parts.text: Strenuous or unfamiliar exercise can cause damage to our muscle fibres. This is particularly the case after doing “eccentric exercises”, where muscles

while generating force. Activities such as downhill running, descending the stairs or lowering a weight under control (while doing a barbell squat for instance) are all examples of eccentric exercise.

This exercise-induced muscle damage can leave your muscles feeling sore and weak. To

the damage, the body triggers what’s known as an “inflammatory repair response”, where immune cells move into the muscle tissue to clear away damaged cellular material and stimulate regeneration.

Other

are also released to help coordinate repair. However, these molecules can also increase the sensitivity of pain receptors, which may further contribute to the muscle soreness that people experience up to 72 hours after an intense workout.

These responses are an important part of how the body repairs itself and

stronger.

We wanted to better understand what effect different recovery methods had on this repair process after a strenuous workout. So we recruited 40 healthy, physically active adults (31 men and nine women) and asked them to

a specific exercise.

This involved repeatedly targeting the quadriceps – the large muscles at the front of the thigh – using a specialised machine that allowed us to carefully control the movement and measure muscle strength. This particular movement is known to cause

muscle damage and soreness – making it useful for studying how different recovery methods influence the body’s repair process.

Participants were then randomly assigned to one of four recovery methods: cold-water

(in water that was 10°C), hot-water immersion (in water that was 42°C), hot air exposure (60°C, similar to a sauna) and “passive recovery” which involved sitting and doing nothing for 30 minutes. Each method was carried out immediately after the workout.

Over the following 72 hours, we

recovery by looking at several measures – including muscle strength, pain and soreness, alongside various biological markers linked to muscle damage, inflammation and cellular stress.

All participants showed the expected signs of exercise-induced muscle damage. Strength

immediately after exercise and soreness increased.

But when we looked at the effects of the recovery techniques, we were surprised to find that none of them restored muscle strength significantly faster than the others.

If strength had been the only
measured, we might have concluded the recovery methods made little difference. But the physiological data told a different story.

They are used by elite athletes and recreational gym-goers to reduce soreness and recuperate more quickly after exercising.
